text: Executing a person who deliberately kills an innocent victim is the only proportionate response to the gravity of that crime.
Life imprisonment is an inadequate punishment for mass murderers and serial killers who show no remorse.
The threat of execution deters some would-be murderers who would not be stopped by a prison sentence.
Families of murder victims deserve the closure that only the execution of the killer can provide.
A society that refuses to execute its worst offenders fails to express the true value it places on innocent life.
Executing a murderer permanently guarantees that the person can never kill again, inside prison or out.
Lethal injection delivers a humane death that is far gentler than the way murder victims die.
Modern DNA evidence has made wrongful convictions in capital cases rare enough to justify keeping the penalty.
Taxpayers should not be forced to feed and house child killers for the rest of their natural lives.
A murderer forfeits his own right to life by deliberately taking the life of another person.
Scripture's principle of a life for a life gives moral authority to the execution of murderers.
Prisoners serving life sentences with no hope of release have little reason not to attack guards and fellow inmates.
The prospect of a death sentence gives prosecutors leverage to obtain confessions and the locations of victims' bodies.
Retribution is a legitimate purpose of criminal law, and execution is its fullest expression for the worst crimes.
Juries sentencing a murderer to death are exercising democratic judgment that deserves respect rather than being overridden by abolitionists.
Terrorists who kill civilians should face execution as a statement that society will not tolerate such atrocities.
Executing killers is no more a violation of human dignity than imprisoning kidnappers, since both punish chosen wrongs.
Countries that carry out executions send a stronger message against violent crime than countries that have abolished them.
A life sentence can be reduced by parole boards or pardons, while execution ensures the sentence is carried out.
Some crimes are so monstrous that no punishment short of death can satisfy the demands of justice.
Every execution risks killing an innocent person, and that irreversible mistake can never be undone or compensated.
The state has no moral authority to take a human life, even the life of a convicted murderer.
Studies comparing states and countries show no reliable evidence that executions reduce homicide rates more than imprisonment does.
Capital cases cost taxpayers far more than life imprisonment because of lengthy trials and mandatory appeals.
Defendants who are poor or belong to racial minorities are far more likely to receive a death sentence for similar crimes.
Life without parole protects the public just as effectively as execution while leaving room to correct mistakes.
Killing a prisoner who is already helpless is revenge dressed up as justice, and it lowers the state to the killer's level.
Botched lethal injections have caused prolonged agony, showing that no method of execution is reliably humane.
Every person retains an inherent right to life that no crime and no government can legitimately remove.
Executions prolong the grief of victims' families by dragging them through decades of appeals and media attention.
Religious teachings on mercy and redemption forbid the state from putting a repentant sinner to death.
Dozens of death row inmates have been exonerated, proving that the justice system convicts innocent people of capital crimes.
Most developed democracies have abolished capital punishment, which marks it as a relic of a less civilized age.
Prison staff and doctors forced to take part in executions suffer lasting psychological harm.
A government that kills its own citizens as punishment teaches the public that killing is an acceptable solution to problems.
Murderers who spend their lives in prison can reflect, repent, and sometimes contribute to the lives of others.
Prosecutors and juries apply the death penalty arbitrarily, so who is executed depends more on geography and luck than on guilt.
Condemned inmates endure years of dread on death row, a form of psychological torture that amounts to cruel punishment.
Money spent on executions would do more good if directed toward crime prevention and support for victims' families.
Abolishing the death penalty reflects moral progress, as societies have gradually rejected torture, mutilation, and public killings.
Polio, smallpox, and many other devastating diseases were brought under control largely thanks to vaccines developed through animal experiments.
Animals experience pain and fear much as humans do, so inflicting suffering on them for human gain is a grave moral wrong.
Humans hold a higher moral status than other species, so human lives rightly take priority over animal welfare.
Every animal is the subject of its own life and holds a right not to be used as a research tool.
Regulated animal testing is the safest way to screen new drugs before they are given to human volunteers.
Results from rodents often fail to predict how drugs behave in humans, which makes animal experiments an unreliable basis for medicine.
Modern oversight committees and welfare laws keep suffering in laboratories to a minimum and make animal research ethically acceptable.
Laboratory animals endure confinement, injury, and death, and no welfare regulation can make that treatment humane.
Computer models and cell cultures cannot yet reproduce a whole living body, so living animals remain necessary for studying complex diseases.
Organ-on-a-chip technology, human tissue cultures, and computer simulation can already replace most animal experiments.
Banning animal research would condemn countless patients to preventable death while sparing animals only a small share of the suffering humans cause.
Society has no right to treat sentient creatures as disposable instruments, just as it has no right to experiment on unwilling humans.
Most major Nobel Prize winning advances in physiology and medicine relied on experiments with animals.
Many drugs that passed animal trials went on to harm or kill people, which proves animal data cannot guarantee human safety.
Animals have no moral duties or rational autonomy, so they cannot hold rights that override the needs of sick humans.
Judging a being's worth by its intelligence or species is a prejudice comparable to racism and sexism.
Religious traditions give humans stewardship over animals, and using them to heal the sick falls within that mandate.
Compassion toward all living creatures is a core religious duty that forbids deliberately causing animals to suffer for profit or curiosity.
Surgeons gain life-saving techniques by practicing and testing procedures on animals before operating on human patients.
Funding spent on animal laboratories would produce better health outcomes if redirected to human-based research and prevention.
Because animal experiments are legally required before human trials, abolishing them would leave drug safety unprotected.
Pharmaceutical companies rely on animal testing mainly to shield themselves from liability, not because it benefits patients.
Animals used in research are bred for that purpose, so their use does not take anything from wild populations or nature.
Millions of animals die in laboratories every year, a mass killing that no medical benefit could excuse.
A researcher who refuses animal experiments when they could cure a disease bears responsibility for the human deaths that follow.
Past abuses in laboratories show that researchers cannot be trusted to police their own treatment of animals.
Genetically engineered mice allow scientists to study cancer and inherited diseases in ways that no other method can match.
Humans differ so much from mice, monkeys, and dogs in biology that findings from those species mislead researchers more than they help.
Reducing, refining, and replacing animals gradually is a sensible path, but total abolition would stall medical progress.
Any medical progress built on torturing the defenseless is morally tainted and should be abandoned.
Veterinary medicine also benefits from animal research, so animals themselves gain from the treatments tested on them.
Animals cannot consent to experiments, so using them is exploitation no matter what humans gain.
Public health depends on animal testing to detect toxic chemicals before they reach consumers, workers, and children.
Cosmetics and household products are tested on animals to little purpose, and this shows research on animals is often trivial and wasteful.
The suffering of a mouse in a lab is a small price compared with the lives saved by the cure it helps produce.
No quantity of human benefit can balance the agony of a monkey locked in a cage and subjected to repeated procedures.
Countries that ban animal experiments would simply import medical advances developed elsewhere, free-riding on the animal research of others.
Phasing out animal research would push scientists to build better human-relevant methods and make medicine more accurate.
Vaccines against COVID-19 reached the public rapidly only because animal studies confirmed their safety and effectiveness first.
Every species that feels pain deserves legal protection from experiments, and laws allowing laboratory use are as unjust as slavery once was.
Offenders convicted of murder should serve life sentences without any possibility of parole.
Mandatory minimum sentences are an effective way to deter serious crime and ensure consistent punishment.
Police officers should be given broader powers to stop and search people in high-crime neighborhoods.
Teenagers who commit violent crimes should be tried and sentenced as adults.
Prison conditions should be deliberately austere so that incarceration serves as a genuine deterrent.
Prisons should focus primarily on rehabilitation and education rather than on punishing offenders.
Possession of drugs for personal use should be decriminalized and treated as a public health issue.
Juvenile offenders should never be sentenced to life imprisonment, regardless of the seriousness of their crime.
Solitary confinement should be banned because it amounts to torture.
Cash bail should be abolished because it punishes poor defendants before they have been convicted of anything.
Eating meat is morally wrong because it causes unnecessary suffering to sentient animals.
Keeping wild animals in zoos is unethical, since captivity cannot meet their natural needs.
Hunting animals for sport is a cruel practice that should be banned.
Testing cosmetics on animals should be illegal everywhere, whatever the commercial consequences.
Animals should be granted legal rights as persons rather than being treated as property.
Using animals for food is a natural and acceptable part of human life.
Zoos play an essential role in conservation and public education that justifies keeping animals in captivity.
Regulated hunting is a legitimate form of wildlife management and a valid recreational tradition.
Owning pets is a fair arrangement, since domesticated animals benefit from human care and companionship.
Animals have no moral standing equal to humans, so human interests should always take priority over theirs.
Governments should phase out nuclear power plants in favor of wind and solar energy, even if electricity costs rise somewhat.
Annual immigration levels should be cut substantially because rapid inflows strain housing, public services, and national social cohesion.
The federal minimum wage should be raised to at least fifteen dollars an hour, even if some jobs are lost as a result.
Rent control reduces housing supply and quality, and cities should abolish it in favor of building more homes.
Modern free trade agreements have mostly hurt ordinary workers, and countries should use tariffs to protect domestic industries.
Public funds should follow students to private and religious schools through vouchers, because families deserve a choice about where their children are educated.
Billionaires should pay an annual tax on their net wealth to reduce concentrated economic and political power.
Editing the genes of human embryos to prevent hereditary disease is morally acceptable and should be permitted under regulation.
Governments should legally require social media companies to remove hateful and misleading content from their platforms.
Physician-assisted dying for terminally ill adults is a fundamental right that every state should legalize.
A strong sense of national identity and patriotism is essential for a healthy and cohesive society.
Governments should spend far less on crewed space exploration and redirect that money to problems on Earth.
Universal government-run health insurance would deliver better and fairer care than the current mix of private and public coverage.
Private gun ownership is a constitutional right that should not be restricted by new federal licensing or registration requirements.
Abortion should be illegal after the first trimester except when the mother's life is in danger.
Governments should prioritize expanding domestic oil and gas production over rapid decarbonization, because affordable energy matters more than aggressive climate targets.
Public universities should forgive most outstanding student loan debt using taxpayer funds.
Welfare benefits should carry work requirements, because employment builds independence better than unconditional aid does.
Traditional marriage between one man and one woman is the best foundation for raising children and stable communities.
Employers and universities should use race-conscious affirmative action to counteract the lasting effects of historical discrimination.
